front: In the nuclear symbol $^{A}_{Z}X^{c}$, how do you find neutrons and electrons?
back: Neutrons = A − Z. Electrons = Z − charge (c). E.g. $^{32}_{16}$S²⁻: 16 p, 16 n, 18 e⁻.

front: Where is the mass and charge of an atom concentrated?
back: Almost all the mass and all the positive charge are in a tiny, dense nucleus (protons + neutrons); electrons occupy the space around it.

front: What did the gold-foil (Rutherford) experiment show?
back: Most α particles passed straight through (atom mostly empty space); a few deflected strongly (small, dense, positive nucleus).

front: Why do isotopes differ in physical but not chemical properties?
back: Chemistry depends on electron configuration (same). Different neutron numbers change mass, so density, rate of diffusion and mp/bp differ slightly.

front: Ar of chlorine from ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%)?
Finding isotope abundances from Ar (two isotopes)?
back: Let abundance of one isotope = x and the other = 100 − x; solve Ar = [m₁x + m₂(100 − x)]/100.

front: Why is Ar rarely a whole number?
back: It is a weighted mean over the naturally occurring isotopes (and isotope masses are not exactly whole numbers).

front: (HL) What a mass spectrometer does to a sample?
back: Vaporises and ionises the atoms (forming positive ions), accelerates and separates them by m/z, then detects them to give relative abundances.

front: (HL) Peaks in the mass spectrum of Cl₂ in the molecular-ion region?
(HL) Calculating Ar from a mass spectrum?
back: Ar = Σ(m/z × relative abundance) ÷ Σ(relative abundances), using each peak.

front: Do electrons contribute to the mass number?
back: No. A counts only protons and neutrons; an electron is ~1/1836 of a proton’s mass, so ions have essentially the same mass as their atoms.
